**Emancipation of the serfs (1861)**
Alexander II's Emancipation Reform freed Russia's serfs, peasants legally bound to the land and their landlords. Freed peasants stayed organized in village communes called mirs (obshchinas) and owed redemption payments for their land until these were abolished in 1907. Exiled writer Alexander Herzen's newspaper The Bell reported on the reform in advance, and new local councils called zemstvos were created to run local affairs.

**Assassination of Alexander II by the People's Will (1881)**
The "Tsar Liberator" was killed by bombs thrown at his carriage in St. Petersburg by the revolutionary group People's Will (Narodnaya Volya), which grew out of the Narodnik populist movement. The Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood stands on the spot; his reign also saw the 1863 January Uprising in Poland and gains of Kars and Batum from the Ottomans in 1878.

**Nicholas II and the execution of the Romanovs**
The last tsar, who abdicated in the February Revolution of 1917. In 1918 the Bolsheviks shot him and his family in Yekaterinburg; some bullets bounced off jewels sewn into the daughters' clothing, which fed myths that Anastasia survived, and Anna Anderson was the most famous of the women who claimed to be her.

**Empress Alexandra and Rasputin**
Nicholas II's wife, a German-born princess, was deeply unpopular for her belief in strict autocracy and her reliance on the mystic Grigori Rasputin, who she believed could ease the hemophilia of her son Alexei.

**Revolution of 1905 and the October Manifesto**
It began on Bloody Sunday (January 1905), when troops fired on a peaceful workers' march led by the priest Father Georgy Gapon. Nicholas II responded with the October Manifesto, which created an elected Duma, followed by the 1906 Fundamental (Basic) Laws. Sergei Witte, architect of Russia's industrialization, became the first prime minister, and the reactionary Black Hundreds carried out violence in the tsar's name.

**Revolutions of 1917**
The February Revolution forced Nicholas II's abdication and ended the Romanov dynasty, leaving a Provisional Government later led by Alexander Kerensky. The October Revolution then overthrew Kerensky and brought Lenin's Bolsheviks to power.

**Peter the Great**
The modernizing tsar who toured Western Europe in the Grand Embassy, created the merit-based Table of Ranks, defeated Charles XII of Sweden at Poltava (1709) in the Great Northern War, and built St. Petersburg on the Baltic. He crushed a streltsy revolt meant to restore his half-sister Sophia, and he put aside his conservative first wife Eudoxia Lopukhina, later taking Anna Mons as a mistress.

**Catherine the Great**
The German-born empress (ruled 1762–1796) who wrote the Nakaz ("Instruction") for a new law code and annexed Crimea. Her favorite Grigory Potemkin supposedly built fake "Potemkin villages" to impress her on a tour of Crimea, and her reign saw Pugachev's Rebellion and Russia's role in starting the First Partition of Poland.

**Empress Elizabeth**
Peter the Great's daughter (ruled 1741–1762), who never carried out a single execution during her reign. Hostile to Prussia, she fought Frederick the Great in the Seven Years' War, and her death prompted the "Miracle of the House of Brandenburg," when her successor Peter III made peace and saved Prussia.

**Ivan III and Ivan IV ("the Terrible")**
Ivan III ("the Great") threw off Mongol overlordship and rebuilt the Moscow Kremlin. Ivan IV (Grozny) created the streltsy musketeers and the oprichnina, a terror apparatus run by the oprichniki, and in 1581 killed his own son with a staff in a fit of rage, which helped end the Rurikid dynasty.

**Time of Troubles**
The chaos from 1598 to 1613 after the Rurikid line died out. It included the elected tsar Boris Godunov, three "False Dmitry" pretenders, and a Polish occupation of Moscow after the Battle of Klushino. Kuzma Minin and Dmitry Pozharsky led the force that drove out the Poles, and the Romanov dynasty began in 1613.

**Alexander Nevsky and Alexander I**
Alexander Nevsky, a Prince of Novgorod, defeated the Teutonic Knights in the 1242 Battle on the Ice while cooperating with the Mongol Golden Horde, and was canonized in 1547. Tsar Alexander I took power after his father Paul I was murdered, signed the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon on a raft in the Neman River in 1807, and employed the reformer Mikhail Speransky.

**Siberia and the Trans-Siberian Railway**
Russia's conquest of Siberia began when the Cossack Yermak defeated Kuchum Khan of the Siberian Khanate in the 1580s. Indigenous peoples paid the yasak tribute in furs, and Siberia became a place of exile and forced labor (katorga). The Trans-Siberian Railway, ending at Vladivostok and routed around Lake Baikal, tied the empire together.

**Bering, the Alaska colony, and the Alaska Purchase**
Peter the Great sponsored Danish-born explorer Vitus Bering's first expedition, and a later expedition (from 1733) included naturalist Georg Steller, namesake of Steller's jay. Russia set up fur-trading colonies in Alaska but sold the territory to the U.S. in 1867 in a deal negotiated by Eduard de Stoeckl and mocked as "Seward's Folly."

**Prehistoric Russia: Denisova Cave, Sintashta, and Beringia**
The Denisovans, an extinct group of archaic humans, are named for a cave in Siberia's Altai Mountains. The Sintashta culture built the earliest known chariots, the Yamnaya culture is linked to the Proto-Indo-Europeans in Marija Gimbutas's Kurgan hypothesis, and the Beringia land bridge let humans migrate from Siberia to the Americas.
